title: Making plans together
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: TY ENTERS HERE, and the level held it back on purpose: a learner who guesses wrong with a stranger is rude, while a learner who guesses wrong with a friend is merely stiff, so L1 taught vy and showed ty in no display at all. Plans are made with friends, which is what pays for it. With ty come tebyá and tebé, the -esh' ending on every verb the course owns, and the singular imperative — skazhí where a stranger got skazhíte.

The move from vy to ty is NEGOTIATED OUT LOUD in Russian — Davay na ty — rather than drifted into. Knowing only that ty is "informal" is what makes a learner switch too early and land somewhere between presumptuous and childish. The real trigger is age and closeness, agreed between the two people, and once agreed it does not go back.

Davay is the suggestion particle and takes the first-person PLURAL of the future: Davay poydyóm, Davay vstrétimsya. Davayte is its vy partner, so the pair drills the module's register point as well as its grammar. English "let's" is one word for both addresses; Russian's carries the address with it.

TIME FORKS BY PREPOSITION. A clock hour takes v — v pyat' chasóv, with L1-M4's chasóv and L1-M8's pyat' already owned. A day takes v too, and there the feminine accusative shows: v subbótu. But a part of the day takes NOTHING: útrom, vécherom, dnyóm, nóch'yu are frozen instrumental forms L1-M4 taught as words, and there is no pattern in them to copy — exactly as M4 said of peshkóm.

Two words that look alike are different kinds of thing. skazhí and skazhíte are ONE verb in two addresses and share a row. skazhíte and govoríte are aspect partners and never share one. The test is simple: if choosing between them is choosing whom you are talking to, it is one word; if it is choosing how the action is presented, it is two.

words.note: Literally "give", used as a suggestion particle. It carries the address with it, which English's "let's" does not.

words.cue: let's (to more than one, or politely)
words.note: davay's vy partner. Same word, different address — so the two share nothing but a stem and are chosen the way skazhí and skazhíte are.
The first-person plural of L1-M5's poydú. Carries a yó and therefore the stress. After davay this is a suggestion, not a prediction.
Indeclinable, like M4's metró and kófe — v kinó whatever the case. It means both the building and the art form.

sentences.trap: davay is followed by a FUTURE, not by an infinitive. Davay idtí is wrong, and the mistake comes straight from English's "let's go", where the verb has no ending at all.
sentences.sound: da-VAY pay-DYOM v ki-NO. Three stresses in a row on the last syllable, which is what makes the line sound like an invitation.

variations.changed: to more than one person, or politely
a different destination, still motion
a different suggestion

mistake.why: davay takes the plural future: Davay poydyóm v kinó.

sentences.usage: Between friends. Said to a stranger it would be presumptuous, and davayte is what that situation needs.
sentences.mnemonic: davay plus we-will, never plus to-do.

words.note: A reflexive verb — the -sya on the end makes it "meet each other". The reflexive system itself is L3's; this arrives as a word.
Feminine, so its accusative shows: v subbótu. Days of the week are not capitalised in Russian, which is the reverse of English.

sentences.trap: The day takes the ACCUSATIVE after v, so subbóta becomes subbótu. It is the same v as M4's motion — Russian treats a day as something you go into.
sentences.sound: da-VAY VSTRYE-tim-sya v su-BO-tu. The vstr cluster starts the word with no vowel, which English mouths want to soften.

variations.changed: a neuter day, so nothing visible changes
the polite address and a masculine day
a part of the day — no preposition at all

mistake.why: A day after v takes the accusative: v subbótu.

sentences.usage: Fixing a day. The hour comes in the next breath.

words.note: For one person you are close to. L1 taught vy for everyone because guessing wrong with a stranger is the costly mistake; this is the module where the other half arrives.
A short-form adjective, like M2's ustál and M5's syt: it agrees with the person and cannot stand in front of a noun.
The feminine short form. Asking a woman with svobóden is heard immediately, and there is no neutral option.

sentences.trap: Which form to use is decided by the person being ASKED, not by the person asking. A man asking a woman says svobódna.
sentences.sound: ty sva-BO-din v su-BO-tu. The stress of both content words falls on the same vowel sound, which makes the question easy to hear.

variations.changed: asking a woman
the polite address, so the plural short form
the answer

mistake.why: The predicate takes the short form: Ty svobóden v subbótu?

sentences.usage: The question that opens every plan between friends.
sentences.mnemonic: The short form agrees with whoever it is about.

words.note: Neuter, so its accusative is the same as its nominative and nothing visible happens after v. The word means "resurrection".
Masculine and inanimate, so its accusative is its nominative too. Literally "the day after the not-doing" — after voskresén'ye.

sentences.trap: Two of the three days shown change nothing after v, and only subbóta does. That is not the days behaving differently — it is the accusative being invisible on neuters and inanimate masculines, exactly as M3 said.
sentences.sound: v vas-kri-SYEN'-ye ya sva-BO-din. Four unstressed vowels in the first word, all reduced.

variations.changed: a masculine day and a different verb
the feminine day, where the ending shows
where rather than whether

mistake.why: A day of the week takes v: V voskresén'ye ya svobóden.

sentences.usage: Answering the question above, or offering a day before being asked.
sentences.mnemonic: Only the feminine day shows its ending.

sentences.cue: At what time? At five o'clock

words.note: A whole surface, beside L1-M8's skól'ko stóit. The vo is v with a vowel added, because v skól'ko would be unsayable — spelling following the mouth.

sentences.trap: chasóv is the genitive plural, and it is there because pyat' is a word of amount — M3's rule, said in L1-M4 without a reason and now explained. The learner has been saying it correctly for two levels.
sentences.sound: va SKOL'-ka? v pyat' cha-SOF. The final v of chasóv goes voiceless, so the word ends in an f.

variations.cue: What time will you be home?
variations.changed: a full question, with L1-M6's future
a different hour, the same genitive plural
the hour inside a suggestion

mistake.why: A cluster takes the longer form: Vo skól'ko?

sentences.usage: The second half of settling a plan, after the day is agreed.
sentences.mnemonic: A cluster ahead means vo, not v.

sentences.cue: Do you want tea or coffee?

words.note: The ty form of the verb L1-M3 taught as khochú and khotíte. The -esh' ending is what every ty form is built on.
The same -esh' ending on a regular verb. Ty znáyesh'? on its own is "you know what?" and opens a piece of news.

sentences.trap: The soft sign on the end of every ty form is not decoration and is not silent — it softens the sh, and dropping it in writing is the commonest slip a learner makes here.
sentences.sound: ty KHO-chish' chay i-li KO-fye. The kh is the Scottish "loch" sound, and the ch that follows is soft.

variations.cue: Do you know where the shop is?
variations.changed: a different verb, and a question inside a question
another -esh' verb

variations.cue: Would you like tea or coffee?
variations.changed: the polite address — L1's form, unchanged

mistake.why: ty takes the -esh' form: Ty khóchesh' chay ili kófe?

sentences.usage: At home with a friend. M5's Vam chay ili kófe? is the same offer to a guest you address as vy.
sentences.mnemonic: ty always ends the verb in -esh'.

words.note: The ty cell of L1-M1's rabótat'. A regular verb, and the ending is the only thing that has changed.
The ty cell of L1-M3's chitát'. Same ending again — this is the point at which the pattern stops needing to be learnt word by word.
The ty cell of L1-M6's búdu and búdete. It also builds the imperfective future, which M10 will need.

sentences.trap: Russian has no separate continuous, so this one question is both "do you work" and "are you working". Only the day at the end says which is meant.
sentences.sound: ty ra-BO-ta-yish' v su-BO-tu. The -yesh' ending is one syllable and easy to swallow; keeping it audible is what makes the address clear.

variations.changed: a different verb, with an accusative object

variations.cue: Will you be at home tomorrow?
variations.changed: the future
the polite address

mistake.why: ty takes -esh': Ty rabótayesh' v subbótu?

sentences.usage: Finding out whether a friend is free, without asking directly.

words.note: The singular imperative. It shares a row with L1-M6's pozvoníte because they are ONE verb in two addresses — unlike an aspect pair, which never shares a row.
M1's skazhíte in the ty address, on the same row for the same reason. Its aspect partner govorí is a different word and lives elsewhere.
L1-M8's dáyte in the ty address. One syllable, so no stress mark — and it is the shortest imperative in the language.

sentences.trap: Dropping the -te is not a shortening; it is a change of address. Saying pozvoní to a stranger is exactly as wrong as saying pozvoníte to a close friend, and only one of the two is rude.
sentences.sound: paz-va-NI mnye ZAV-tra pa-ZHA-lsta. Both o's of pozvoní reduce, so only the last syllable carries.

variations.changed: a different verb in the same address
the shortest imperative, with an accusative object
the polite address — the -te is back

mistake.why: The address has to match: Pozvoní mne závtra or Pozvoníte mne závtra.

sentences.usage: Between friends. Even here pozháluysta is normal — the address is informal, the request still polite.
sentences.mnemonic: -te is not politeness. It is plural, and vy borrows it.

sentences.cue: I'll call you in the evening

words.note: The dative of ty, beside M1's mne and L1-M2's vam. pozvonít' takes the dative, exactly as pomóch' does.
The accusative and genitive of ty, beside L1-M1's menyá. Ya tebyá ne ponimáyu is the sentence it turns up in most.

sentences.trap: vécherom takes no preposition at all. It is a frozen instrumental, a word rather than a pattern — the same warning M4 gave about peshkóm, and the instrumental proper is still L3's.
sentences.sound: ya ti-BYE paz-va-NYU VYE-chi-ram. Only vécherom is stressed on its first syllable; everything else runs late.

variations.changed: the object form instead of the dative

variations.cue: I'll call you in the evening
variations.changed: the polite address
two time words, neither with a preposition

mistake.why: A part of the day takes no preposition: Ya tebé pozvonyú vécherom.

sentences.usage: Closing a plan with a promise to confirm it.
sentences.mnemonic: Parts of the day take nothing at all.

words.note: M4's do plus L1-M6's závtra, riding as one farewell. L1-M1's do svidániya is built the same way — "until the seeing again".

sentences.trap: khoroshó has been in the course since L1-M2 meaning "well". Here it means "all right, agreed", which is a second job and not a second word — its row admits both.
sentences.sound: kha-ra-SHO da ZAV-tra. Both o's of khoroshó reduce to a, so only the last one is fully sounded.

variations.cue: All right, see you on Saturday!
variations.changed: a day, in the genitive after do

variations.cue: All right, see you on Sunday!
variations.changed: a neuter day, and its genitive does show
the farewell alone

mistake.why: do takes the genitive: do subbóty.

sentences.usage: Ending the conversation that made the plan.
sentences.mnemonic: do means until, and takes the genitive.

Do you want tea or coffee?
I'll call you in the evening
Will you be at home tomorrow?
